chapters.synopsisKo: 학교로 가던 피노키오는 인형극 음악에 마음을 빼앗겨, 제페토가 외투를 팔아 마련한 책을 입장료와 바꾼다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Begin with sincere hopeful plans, let the distant music become increasingly irresistible, and end with a sober reminder of Geppetto shivering at home.
chapters.artBrief: A wide village-road panorama linking the school path to a colorful but original wooden marionette theater. Pinocchio carries the A-B-C book, musicians and a small crowd draw him sideways, and a ragpicker waits near the ticket entrance while a cold path points back toward Geppetto's home.

foundation: Pinocchio walked to school with his new book.
He dreamed of helping Geppetto one day.
Then he heard pipes and drums nearby.
The music came from a puppet theater.
A ticket cost four pennies.
Pinocchio had no money for the show.
He sold his A-B-C book to a ragpicker.
At home, Geppetto still shivered without his coat.
core: Pinocchio hurried toward school with the new A-B-C book under his arm.
He imagined learning quickly and buying Geppetto a magnificent coat.
Distant pipes and drums interrupted those generous plans.
He discovered that the music announced a Great Marionette Theater.
Although school waited in the other direction, curiosity pulled him toward the crowd.
The ticket cost four pennies, and Pinocchio did not own even one.
He tried to sell his paper coat, bark shoes, and dough cap.
When nobody wanted them, he finally offered the A-B-C book.
A ragpicker paid four pennies, and Pinocchio entered the theater.
Meanwhile, Geppetto shivered at home after selling his coat for that very book.
studio: Pinocchio set out for school rehearsing splendid plans to learn, earn money, and reward Geppetto with a jeweled coat.
His gratitude sounded sincere until the distant rhythm of pipes and drums introduced a more immediate temptation.
At the crossing, school demanded patience in one direction while the marionette theater promised excitement in the other.
Pinocchio postponed responsibility with the convenient belief that tomorrow would always provide enough time for study.
He reached a brilliant wooden theater whose performance was beginning behind a crowd of eager spectators.
The entrance fee was only four pennies, yet it exceeded everything the penniless marionette owned.
His flowered-paper coat, bark shoes, and dough cap proved too useless even for another child to buy.
After hesitation, curiosity defeated gratitude and he offered the A-B-C book purchased through his father's sacrifice.
A ragpicker exchanged four pennies for the book, turning Geppetto's winter coat into a single afternoon of entertainment.
As Pinocchio rushed inside, the narrator leaves us with the image of his father shivering at home in shirt sleeves.

chapters.synopsisKo: 극장의 인형들은 피노키오를 형제로 환영하지만 공연이 엉망이 되고, 무서운 단장 불먹보가 그를 불쏘시개로 쓰려 한다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Make the reunion exuberant and musical, then cut the warmth sharply when Fire Eater appears. His threat should feel theatrical and frightening without becoming graphic.
chapters.artBrief: An original traveling marionette theater shown as a wide stage-and-backstage panorama: Harlequin and Pulcinella under warm footlights, Pinocchio leaping from audience to stage, a cheering wooden troupe, and a dark kitchen arch where the enormous bearded Fire Eater appears beside a cooking fire.

foundation: Pinocchio entered the crowded puppet theater.
The wooden actors recognized him as a brother.
They stopped the play and cheered loudly.
Pinocchio jumped onto the stage with them.
Then the frightening director appeared.
His name was Fire Eater.
He needed more wood for his cooking fire.
Fire Eater ordered the puppets to bring Pinocchio.
core: Pinocchio slipped inside while Harlequin and Pulcinella performed onstage.
The wooden actors suddenly recognized him and called him their brother.
Their joyful welcome stopped the play and angered the waiting audience.
Pinocchio leaped across the seats and joined the celebration onstage.
The noise ended when the theater's enormous director appeared.
Fire Eater had a black beard, burning eyes, and a dangerous whip.
After the show, he went to the kitchen where a lamb cooked over a fire.
Because the fire needed wood, he remembered the newly arrived marionette.
He ordered Harlequin and Pulcinella to carry Pinocchio into the kitchen.
Terrified, Pinocchio cried for Geppetto and begged not to die.
studio: Pinocchio entered the theater while Harlequin and Pulcinella exchanged their usual comic threats beneath the stage lights.
The performance stopped the instant the wooden actors recognized a living marionette among the spectators.
Calling him their brother, the entire company abandoned the script and invited Pinocchio into a thunderous reunion.
He bounded from audience to orchestra to stage, where the delighted troupe carried him around in triumph.
The celebration vanished when the director emerged with a floor-length black beard, glowing eyes, and an enormous whip.
Fire Eater's presence reduced the noisy theater to a silence so complete that even a passing fly might be heard.
When the show ended, the director returned to a kitchen where his supper still turned above an underfed fire.
Needing seasoned wood, he decided that the unexpected marionette would make excellent fuel.
Harlequin and Pulcinella obeyed in fear and carried their struggling new brother toward the fire.
The chapter closes with Pinocchio calling desperately for the father whose gift he had abandoned.

chapters.synopsisKo: 불먹보는 피노키오 대신 할리퀸을 태우려 하지만, 피노키오가 친구를 위해 자신을 내놓자 감동해 모두를 살려 준다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Balance Fire Eater's comic sneezing with real moral tension. Pinocchio's offer must sound clear and brave, not melodramatic, and the ending should release into warm communal celebration.
chapters.artBrief: The theater kitchen and stage in one wide paper set: huge Fire Eater in a chair near the low fire, Pinocchio and frightened Harlequin at center, two wooden officers nearby, and bright stage lanterns waiting on the far side for the final celebration.

foundation: Fire Eater felt sorry for Pinocchio.
Whenever he felt sad, he sneezed loudly.
He decided not to burn Pinocchio.
Instead, he ordered Harlequin into the fire.
Pinocchio begged him to spare his friend.
He offered to take Harlequin's place.
Fire Eater admired Pinocchio's courage.
He freed them both, and the puppets celebrated.
core: Fire Eater began sneezing because Pinocchio's fear made him feel sorry.
The other marionettes knew that each sneeze revealed his softer heart.
He spared Pinocchio but still needed wood to finish his dinner.
Therefore, he ordered two officers to throw Harlequin into the fire.
Pinocchio fell at the director's feet and begged for his friend's life.
Fire Eater refused because someone had to replace the missing firewood.
Pinocchio stood up and offered himself rather than let Harlequin die.
His brave choice moved every wooden actor, including the officers.
Fire Eater softened, embraced Pinocchio, and pardoned Harlequin too.
With everyone safe, the marionettes danced and sang until dawn.
studio: Despite his terrifying appearance, Fire Eater weakened when Pinocchio's cries awakened genuine pity in him.
His compassion revealed itself through enormous sneezes, a habit the frightened marionettes recognized as hopeful news.
He agreed to spare Pinocchio, yet immediately transferred the danger to Harlequin so that his supper could finish cooking.
The wooden officers seized Harlequin, whose fear made his legs collapse beneath him.
Pinocchio abandoned self-preservation and pleaded repeatedly for mercy on behalf of his innocent friend.
When Fire Eater insisted that a substitute must burn, the marionette rose and made his duty clear.
He offered his own body to the flames rather than accept a rescue purchased by Harlequin's death.
The courage of that choice dissolved the director's remaining hardness and moved the entire wooden company to tears.
Fire Eater embraced Pinocchio, granted Harlequin a pardon, and accepted an imperfectly cooked dinner.
Relief transformed the stage into a festival, where the reunited marionettes danced and sang until morning.

chapters.titleEn: The Fox, the Cat, and Five Gold Pieces
chapters.titleKo: 여우와 고양이, 그리고 금화 다섯 닢
chapters.synopsisKo: 아버지에게 줄 금화를 받은 피노키오는 여우와 고양이의 거짓 투자 이야기에 속아 집으로 돌아가려던 결심을 버린다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Open with generous relief, make the Fox smooth and persuasive and the Cat's repetition faintly comic, sharpen the Blackbird warning, and end with the uneasy confidence of a successful con.
chapters.artBrief: A wide country-road panorama from the theater gate toward Geppetto's distant home: Pinocchio holds five gold pieces, a limping russet Fox and supposedly blind gray Cat flank him, a Blackbird warns from a fence, and an imagined golden tree glows like a tempting paper cutout on the horizon.

foundation: Fire Eater gave Pinocchio five gold pieces.
The money was a gift for Geppetto.
On the road, Pinocchio met a Fox and Cat.
They pretended to be lame and blind.
A Blackbird warned Pinocchio not to listen.
The Fox promised a tree full of gold.
Pinocchio wanted to make his money grow.
He forgot Geppetto and followed the strangers.
core: Fire Eater gave Pinocchio five gold pieces to carry home to Geppetto.
Pinocchio planned to buy his father a coat and replace the schoolbook.
Along the road, he met a limping Fox and a supposedly blind Cat.
The sight of the coins briefly made the Fox's paw and the Cat's eyes work.
A Blackbird warned Pinocchio that their advice would bring regret.
The Fox claimed that buried coins could grow into a tree of gold.
At first, Pinocchio refused because his father was waiting at home.
The Fox described thousands of coins and mocked the choice to study.
Greed made the impossible promise sound reasonable to the inexperienced puppet.
Forgetting his father and every good resolution, Pinocchio followed the pair.
studio: The next morning, Fire Eater learned of Geppetto's poverty and entrusted Pinocchio with five gold pieces for his father.
The delighted marionette set out planning both a warm coat for Geppetto and a new A-B-C book for himself.
Before he had traveled far, a limping Fox and a blind Cat greeted him with suspicious knowledge of his family.
The ring of gold momentarily restored the Fox's lame paw and opened the Cat's supposedly sightless eyes, though Pinocchio noticed neither clue.
A Blackbird delivered a direct warning, but the Cat silenced the honest voice and immediately resumed the performance of blindness.
The Fox then offered an effortless fortune: coins planted in the Field of Wonders would grow into a tree heavy with gold.
Pinocchio initially remembered Geppetto, the lost schoolbook, and the pain already caused by disobedience.
Yet the promise of thousands of coins transformed caution into calculation and greed into imagined generosity.
The Fox pretended to want nothing for himself, while the Cat echoed every lie as though repetition were proof.
Convinced that the swindlers were good people, Pinocchio turned away from home and placed himself in their hands.
